description: We are a passionate and ambitious team of students eager to explore space, technology, and innovation. We enjoy solving complex problems, thinking creatively, and turning ideas into impactful solutions. Our interests include programming, artificial intelligence, data science, design, and scientific research. We are looking for motivated, creative, and collaborative team members who are ready to learn, share ideas, and push boundaries to create something extraordinary.
summary:
AstroQuest is an interactive educational space mission simulator designed to introduce children aged 7–12 to the challenges of space exploration through engaging, decision-based gameplay.
Players choose a spacecraft, prepare limited cargo, assemble an astronaut crew, and manage an outpost on the Moon or a Mars-themed training environment. Throughout a ten-day mission, they must balance oxygen, supplies, crew safety, and energy while responding to unpredictable space-weather events.
Our game integrates archived NASA DONKI space-weather data to create meaningful environmental challenges and references NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) to introduce 32 collectible space-biology discoveries.
Through interactive crew assignments, scientific research, equipment upgrades, expeditions, and animated mission events, Apollo-gists transforms complex space-science concepts into accessible learning experiences.
Our goal is to encourage scientific curiosity, critical thinking, resource management, and problem-solving while demonstrating the importance of teamwork and informed decision-making in space missions.
details:
Overview

AstroQuest is an interactive, browser-based educational game developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge.

Our objective is to make space science accessible and enjoyable for children aged 7–12 by transforming real scientific information into interactive missions where every decision matters.

Rather than presenting scientific concepts through traditional lessons, our game allows children to experience the responsibilities of managing a space outpost.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/HamzaBenismail/AstroQuest

How Our Game Works

The experience begins with players selecting one of four spacecraft designs, each featuring a different internal department arrangement. Players then choose their destination, prepare a limited cargo loadout, and assemble a crew of up to six astronauts.

Once the spacecraft lands, players must manage six essential departments:

  • Life Support: Maintains breathable air and supports crew recovery.
  • Greenhouse: Produces food to support the crew's supplies.
  • Power Station: Manages energy generation and battery storage.
  • Science Laboratory: Generates Research Points and enables scientific discoveries.
  • Storm Shelter: Protects crew readiness during dangerous space-weather events.
  • Communications: Provides advice from Earth to support mission decisions.

Astronauts can be dragged into departments, with matching colors and specialties helping children understand their responsibilities. Players allocate limited energy to staffed departments, manage resources, purchase upgrades, and organize expeditions.

Throughout the ten-day mission, players encounter space-weather challenges based on archived NASA data. They receive imperfect forecasts and must prepare their spacecraft without knowing exactly what will happen.

Successful missions require maintaining adequate resources and crew safety. At the end, players receive a mission report explaining their achievements and the consequences of their decisions.

Integration of NASA Data

Our project incorporates two principal NASA resources.

NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database): We use archived solar-flare and space-weather records to generate the environmental challenges encountered during gameplay. These real events are translated into simplified gameplay severity levels, rather than presented as measured radiation exposure.

NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR): We reference NASA's space-biology research collection to introduce 32 collectible scientific discoveries. Topics include growing plants in space, muscle and bone health, microorganisms, radiation research, and biological adaptation.

Scientific discoveries provide additional Research Points when the appropriate Science Lab specialist conducts experiments. Each discovery includes a short educational explanation and a related scientific photograph.

NASA data is retrieved during development and embedded into the game, allowing the application to run without requiring live API access.

Technology and Development

Apollo-gists was developed using:

  • React and JavaScript for interactive interfaces and game-state management.
  • Vite for efficient frontend development and production builds.
  • HTML and CSS for responsive layouts, animations, and visual effects.
  • SVG artwork for spacecraft, astronauts, and interactive departments.
  • Vitest for testing resource calculations, gameplay mechanics, and application behavior.
  • NASA Open APIs and OSDR resources for scientific data acquisition and research references.

The game runs directly in a web browser without requiring user accounts, a backend server, or installation.

Creativity and Educational Value

Our approach combines resource-management gameplay with accessible visuals, interactive astronaut assignments, collectible scientific discoveries, and cinematic animations.

Children learn through experimentation: allocating too much energy to one department reduces what remains for others, while investing in research can improve future performance.

The game rewards strategic thinking rather than memorization. Players can learn from unsuccessful missions, revise their strategies, and try again.

We also incorporated three selectable visual themes, simplified resource icons, color-coded departments, contextual feedback, and reduced-motion support to accommodate different preferences and accessibility needs.

Intended Impact

Apollo-gists aims to inspire younger audiences to explore science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) through an engaging introduction to space exploration.

By connecting authentic NASA research with meaningful gameplay decisions, we hope to strengthen children's scientific curiosity, problem-solving skills, resource-management abilities, and understanding of the challenges involved in keeping astronauts safe.

Our central message is simple: successful space exploration requires preparation, scientific knowledge, teamwork, and careful decisions.
